Integrated plant-science and crop-growth case study

Source: vignettes/v11-plant-science-case-study.Rmd
v11-plant-science-case-study.Rmd

Scientific setting

The synthetic plant_growth dataset links biomass to morphological and physiological indicators: leaf area, SPAD chlorophyll index, leaf N, stomatal conductance, plant height, root mass and specific leaf area. The workflow illustrates how multiple regression can combine measurements from plant nutrition, physiology and growth analysis.

d <- mr_example_data("plant_growth")
head(d)
#>   biomass_g leaf_area_cm2 chlorophyll_spad leaf_N_pct stomatal_conductance

#> 2  26.80686      63.87120         40.46530   3.007287            0.3568904

Explanatory reference model 

fit <- mr_fit(
  biomass_g ~ leaf_area_cm2 + chlorophyll_spad + leaf_N_pct +
    stomatal_conductance + plant_height_cm + root_mass_g +
    specific_leaf_area_cm2_g,
  d,
  goal = "explanation"
)
summary(fit)

A slope represents a conditional association. For example, the leaf-N slope is the expected biomass difference associated with a one-unit difference in leaf N when the other included physiological and morphological variables are held fixed. This conditional quantity can differ from the marginal correlation between leaf N and biomass.

Model adequacy 

mr_diagnose(fit)$fit
#>              n              p effective_rank    residual_df             R2 
#>    160.0000000      7.0000000      8.0000000    152.0000000      0.7055776 
#>    adjusted_R2          sigma            AIC            BIC 
#>      0.6920187      1.3627032    562.8839280    590.5604923
mr_diagnose(fit)$heteroscedasticity
#>    statistic           df      p.value 
#> 21.399450683  7.000000000  0.003221809
mr_diagnose(fit)$specification
#>    statistic          df1          df2      p.value 
#> 8.598484e+00 2.000000e+00 1.500000e+02 2.915511e-04

The three calls emphasize that fit, residual variance and functional form are separate aspects of adequacy.

A plant with an unusual combination of leaf area, conductance and root mass may have high leverage even if its biomass is not an obvious univariate outlier. This is why influence diagnostics are multivariate.

Collinearity among plant traits 

co <- mr_collinearity(fit)
co$VIF
#>                       term      VIF tolerance flag_vif5 flag_vif10
#> 1            leaf_area_cm2 1.023202 0.9773243     FALSE      FALSE
#> 2         chlorophyll_spad 1.033957 0.9671583     FALSE      FALSE
#> 3               leaf_N_pct 1.013308 0.9868669     FALSE      FALSE
#> 4     stomatal_conductance 1.038567 0.9628651     FALSE      FALSE
#> 5          plant_height_cm 1.028080 0.9726870     FALSE      FALSE
#> 6              root_mass_g 1.029847 0.9710178     FALSE      FALSE
#> 7 specific_leaf_area_cm2_g 1.012667 0.9874915     FALSE      FALSE
head(co$correlations, 10)
#>                   term1                    term2 correlation abs_correlation
#> 14 stomatal_conductance              root_mass_g -0.14883918      0.14883918
#> 1         leaf_area_cm2         chlorophyll_spad  0.10804384      0.10804384
#> 8      chlorophyll_spad          plant_height_cm -0.10268295      0.10268295
#> 10 stomatal_conductance          plant_height_cm -0.08746013      0.08746013
#> 5      chlorophyll_spad     stomatal_conductance -0.06685393      0.06685393
#> 18           leaf_N_pct specific_leaf_area_cm2_g  0.06643329      0.06643329
#> 15      plant_height_cm              root_mass_g  0.06516619      0.06516619
#> 2         leaf_area_cm2               leaf_N_pct -0.05858773      0.05858773
#> 16        leaf_area_cm2 specific_leaf_area_cm2_g  0.05800915      0.05800915
#> 7         leaf_area_cm2          plant_height_cm  0.05242760      0.05242760

Growth traits often share biological information. High collinearity can make it difficult to separate a unique plant-height effect from a leaf-area effect even when the two traits jointly predict biomass well.

Importance views

Use the names of the measures in reporting. A standardized slope is not the same quantity as unique explained variance.

Marginal effects 

if (requireNamespace("marginaleffects", quietly = TRUE)) {
  mr_effects(fit, variables = "leaf_N_pct")
  mr_effects(fit, variables = "chlorophyll_spad")
  mr_effects(fit, variables = "stomatal_conductance")
}
#> 
#>  Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>      8.24       1.49 5.54   <0.001 25.0  5.32   11.2
#> 
#> Term: stomatal_conductance
#> Type: response
#> Comparison: dY/dX

Robust-regression sensitivity 

rob <- mr_fit(
  biomass_g ~ leaf_area_cm2 + chlorophyll_spad + leaf_N_pct +
    stomatal_conductance + plant_height_cm + root_mass_g +
    specific_leaf_area_cm2_g,
  d,
  engine = "robust"
)
cbind(OLS = coef(fit), Robust = coef(rob))
#>                                   OLS       Robust
#> (Intercept)               1.501603671  1.028300475
#> leaf_area_cm2             0.148576349  0.156714957
#> chlorophyll_spad          0.177283054  0.175705227
#> leaf_N_pct                1.488846220  1.634891187
#> stomatal_conductance      8.237029137  8.508563455
#> plant_height_cm           0.025958267  0.022595455
#> root_mass_g               0.092846714  0.096991623
#> specific_leaf_area_cm2_g -0.002550005 -0.002964307

Large changes suggest that a small number of observations may be influential. Agreement does not prove the absence of influence, but it provides useful sensitivity evidence.

Regularization for prediction 

pred <- mr_fit(
  biomass_g ~ leaf_area_cm2 + chlorophyll_spad + leaf_N_pct +
    stomatal_conductance + plant_height_cm + root_mass_g +
    specific_leaf_area_cm2_g,
  d,
  goal = "prediction"
)
if (requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ridge <- mr_regularize(pred, "ridge", nfolds = 5, seed = 81)
  lasso <- mr_regularize(pred, "lasso", nfolds = 5, seed = 81)
  enet <- mr_regularize(pred, "elastic_net", alpha = 0.5,
                        nfolds = 5, seed = 81)
  lasso$selected
  enet$selected
}
#> [1] "leaf_area_cm2"        "chlorophyll_spad"     "leaf_N_pct"          
#> [4] "stomatal_conductance" "plant_height_cm"      "root_mass_g"

Out-of-fold predictive performance 

cv <- mr_validate(pred, v = 5, repeats = 4, seed = 82)
cv$summary
#>                  metric      mean         sd
#> 1                  RMSE 1.4109885 0.03192195
#> 2                   MAE 1.1340531 0.01922401
#> 3                    R2 0.6676020 0.01510631
#> 4 calibration_intercept 0.5903227 0.31606839
#> 5     calibration_slope 0.9755250 0.01267641

The model should be described as predictive only on the basis of these out-of-sample predictions or an independent test dataset, not the training R-squared.

Reduced sensor set

Suppose chlorophyll, leaf N, plant height and leaf area are relatively easy to collect, while stomatal conductance and root mass are expensive or destructive. A smaller predictive model can be evaluated as an operational alternative.

reduced <- mr_fit(
  biomass_g ~ leaf_area_cm2 + chlorophyll_spad + leaf_N_pct + plant_height_cm,
  d,
  goal = "prediction"
)
mr_compare(full = pred, reduced = reduced,
           v = 5, repeats = 3, seed = 83)$prediction
#>      model engine                metric      mean          sd note
#> 1     full    ols                  RMSE 1.4188189 0.034067993 <NA>
#> 2     full    ols                   MAE 1.1390627 0.020094030 <NA>
#> 3     full    ols                    R2 0.6639023 0.016129883 <NA>
#> 4     full    ols calibration_intercept 0.7182523 0.227272804 <NA>
#> 5     full    ols     calibration_slope 0.9703468 0.008952746 <NA>
#> 6  reduced    ols                  RMSE 1.5503998 0.040299410 <NA>
#> 7  reduced    ols                   MAE 1.2480850 0.027725740 <NA>
#> 8  reduced    ols                    R2 0.5986460 0.020849435 <NA>
#> 9  reduced    ols calibration_intercept 0.6619194 0.348847278 <NA>
#> 10 reduced    ols     calibration_slope 0.9728611 0.014121136 <NA>

A small loss in accuracy may be acceptable if field measurement becomes much simpler. That trade-off should be described explicitly rather than disguised as a purely statistical model-selection decision.

Bootstrap coefficient stability 

b <- mr_bootstrap(fit, R = 220, type = "pairs", seed = 84)
b$intervals
#>                                 lower       median        upper
#> (Intercept)              -1.289238773  1.736811027  4.516782359
#> leaf_area_cm2             0.117457195  0.149084683  0.174694347
#> chlorophyll_spad          0.140916040  0.177281729  0.217737704
#> leaf_N_pct                1.005332464  1.464010289  1.919972745
#> stomatal_conductance      5.437649246  8.408483034 10.813200104
#> plant_height_cm           0.008028833  0.026056671  0.043516753
#> root_mass_g               0.036378544  0.094381797  0.145576001
#> specific_leaf_area_cm2_g -0.009192344 -0.002447451  0.004229883
sort(b$sign_stability)
#> specific_leaf_area_cm2_g              (Intercept)            leaf_area_cm2 
#>                0.7681818                0.8545455                1.0000000 
#>         chlorophyll_spad               leaf_N_pct     stomatal_conductance 
#>                1.0000000                1.0000000                1.0000000 
#>          plant_height_cm              root_mass_g 
#>                1.0000000                1.0000000

Integrated recommendation 

mr_recommend(fit)
#>               domain                                                finding
#> 1       collinearity No strong VIF signal under the package screening rule.
#> 2 heteroscedasticity                   Breusch-Pagan screening p = 0.00322.
#> 3    functional_form  Fitted-value-power specification screen p = 0.000292.
#> 4          influence   11 observation(s) exceed Cook's 4/n screening value.
#> 5          selection            The declared goal is explanation/inference.
#>                                                                                                                                                                recommendation
#> 1                                                                                          Still inspect correlated predictor groups when scientific redundancy is plausible.
#> 2                                    Keep the mean model if scientifically appropriate, but compare classical inference with HC3/HC4 and consider wild bootstrap sensitivity.
#> 3 Inspect residual patterns and scientifically plausible nonlinear terms; compare polynomial, GAM or kernel sensitivity analyses rather than adding complexity automatically.
#> 4                                                                          Inspect leverage, DFFITS and DFBETAS; conduct sensitivity analysis rather than automatic deletion.
#> 5                                                           Treat automated selection as exploratory; prioritize prespecified scientific terms, effect sizes and uncertainty.
#>   priority
#> 1      low
#> 2     high
#> 3     high
#> 4   medium
#> 5     high

The output is intended to support a methods discussion: whether traits are redundant, whether robust regression changes conclusions, whether the mean functional form is adequate and whether predictive claims have been validated.

Reporting language

A plant-science manuscript should identify the experimental unit, growth stage, measurement method and units for each predictor. Statistical results should emphasize effect estimates and uncertainty, avoid causal language unsupported by design, and distinguish explanatory models from sensor-based predictive models.
